claims.text: What the image looks like Periventricular ovoid T2/FLAIR lesions perpendicular to ventricles ('Dawson fingers'); lesions disseminated in time/space → multiple sclerosis
claims.quote: Periventricular ovoid T2/FLAIR lesions perpendicular to ventricles ('Dawson fingers'); lesions disseminated in time/space Multiple sclerosis
claims.locator: MRI - When MRI > CT, findings table

claims.text: Buzzword: Dawson fingers on brain MRI T2/FLAIR → multiple sclerosis
claims.quote: Dawson fingers Brain MRI T2/FLAIR Multiple sclerosis

claims.text: Example FLAIR MRI (sagittal): multiple hyperintense white matter lesions in a patient with multiple sclerosis, a finding sometimes called Dawson fingers
claims.quote: This image shows multiple hyperintense white matter lesions seen in a sagittal view of the brain of a patient with multiple sclerosis. This finding is sometimes called Dawson fingers.

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Brain: MS plaques, ischemic stroke beyond the first hours (DWI), posterior fossa, tumor characterization, dementia workup
claims.quote: Brain: MS plaques, ischemic stroke beyond first hours (DWI), posterior fossa, tumor characterization, dementia workup.

claims.text: MRI is the most sensitive imaging test for MS and can exclude other treatable disorders that may mimic MS (eg, nondemyelinating lesions at the junction of the spinal cord and medulla); gadolinium contrast enhancement can distinguish actively inflamed from older plaques
claims.quote: MRI is the most sensitive imaging test for MS and can exclude other treatable disorders that may mimic MS, such as nondemyelinating lesions at the junction of the spinal cord and medulla (eg, subarachnoid cyst, foramen magnum tumors). Gadolinium contrast enhancement can distinguish actively inflamed from older plaques.

claims.text: Diagnosis requires a clinical episode consistent with MS (such as optic neuritis, partial myelitis or internuclear ophthalmoplegia) plus evidence of CNS lesions separated in both time and space
claims.quote: The diagnosis of MS requires a clinical episode consistent with MS (such as optic neuritis, partial myelitis or internuclear ophthalmoplegia) plus evidence of CNS lesions that are separated in both time and space (location in the CNS).

claims.text: Separation in time can be indicated by any of: a history of exacerbations and remissions; MRI showing simultaneous enhancing and nonenhancing lesions, even if patients are asymptomatic; a new lesion on a subsequent MRI in patients with a previous lesion
claims.quote: For example, any of the following can indicate separation in time: A history of exacerbations and remissions MRI that shows simultaneous enhancing and nonenhancing lesions, even if patients are asymptomatic A new lesion on a subsequent MRI in patients with a previous lesion

claims.text: Separation in space can be established by lesions in ≥ 2 of the 5 CNS areas typically affected: periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, optic nerve (≥ 1 lesions each; optic nerve by MRI or clinical evaluation)
claims.quote: Separation (dissemination) in space can be established by finding lesions in ≥ 2 of the 5 following CNS areas typically affected by MS (1): Periventricular: ≥ 1 lesions (2) Cortical/juxtacortical (white matter next to cortex and/or cortex): ≥ 1 lesions Infratentorial: ≥ 1 lesions Spinal cord: ≥ 1 lesions Optic nerve: ≥ 1 lesions (either by MRI or clinical evaluation)

claims.text: Causes Believed to involve an immunologic mechanism; one postulated cause is infection by a latent virus (possibly a human herpesvirus such as Epstein-Barr virus) that, when activated, triggers a secondary autoimmune response
claims.quote: Multiple sclerosis is believed to involve an immunologic mechanism. One postulated cause is infection by a latent virus (possibly a human herpesvirus such as Epstein-Barr virus), which, when activated, triggers a secondary autoimmune response.

claims.text: Increased incidence in certain families and HLA allotypes (HLA-DR2) suggest genetic susceptibility
claims.quote: An increased incidence among certain families and presence of human leukocyte antigen (HLA) allotypes (HLA-DR2) suggests genetic susceptibility.

claims.text: Mechanism: localized areas of demyelination (plaques) with destruction of oligodendroglia and perivascular inflammation; axonal damage is common, and neuronal cell bodies may also die or be damaged
claims.quote: Localized areas of demyelination (plaques) occur, with destruction of oligodendroglia, perivascular inflammation, and chemical changes in lipid and protein constituents of myelin in and around the plaques. Axonal damage is common, and neuronal cell bodies may also die or be damaged.

claims.text: Plaques are disseminated throughout the CNS, primarily in white matter, particularly the lateral and posterior columns (especially cervical), optic nerves and periventricular areas
claims.quote: Astrogliosis develops in plaques that are disseminated throughout the central nervous system (CNS), primarily in white matter, particularly in the lateral and posterior columns (especially in the cervical regions), optic nerves, and periventricular areas.

claims.text: Symptoms Most common initial symptoms: paresthesias in one or more extremities, the trunk or one side of the face; weakness or clumsiness of a leg or hand; visual disturbances (eg, partial loss of vision and pain in one eye from retrobulbar optic neuritis, diplopia from internuclear ophthalmoplegia, scotomas)
claims.quote: The most common initial symptoms of multiple sclerosis are the following: Paresthesias in one or more extremities, in the trunk, or on one side of the face Weakness or clumsiness of a leg or hand Visual disturbances (eg, partial loss of vision and pain in one eye due to retrobulbar optic neuritis, diplopia due to internuclear ophthalmoplegia, scotomas)

claims.text: Relapsing-remitting pattern: exacerbations alternate with remissions, when partial or full recovery occurs or symptoms are stable
claims.quote: Relapsing-remitting pattern: Exacerbations alternate with remissions, when partial or full recovery occurs or symptoms are stable.

claims.text: Most patients have difficulty with bladder control (eg, frequency, urgency, hesitancy, incontinence, retention); fatigue is common; excess heat (eg, warm weather, a hot bath, fever) may temporarily exacerbate symptoms and signs (Uhthoff phenomenon)
claims.quote: Most patients with MS have difficulty with bladder control (eg, frequency, urgency, hesitancy, incontinence, retention). Fatigue is common. Excess heat (eg, warm weather, a hot bath, fever) may temporarily exacerbate symptoms and signs (Uhthoff phenomenon).

claims.text: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus): on horizontal gaze, adduction of one eye is decreased with nystagmus of the other (abducting) eye, convergence intact; in MS it is typically bilateral (unilateral is often caused by ischemic stroke)
claims.quote: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia results if there is a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus connecting the nuclei of cranial nerves III, IV, and VI. During horizontal gaze, adduction of 1 eye is decreased, with nystagmus of the other (abducting) eye; convergence is intact. Internuclear ophthalmoplegia in MS is typically bilateral; unilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia is often caused by ischemic stroke.

claims.text: Lhermitte sign: an electric shocklike pain that radiates down the spine or into the legs or arms when the neck is flexed
claims.quote: An example is Lhermitte sign, an electric shocklike pain that radiates down the spine or into the legs or arms when the neck is flexed.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: DMT (ocrelizumab, etc.); MRI brain & spine
claims.quote: DMT (ocrelizumab, etc.); MRI brain & spine
claims.locator: MRI - When MRI > CT, findings table

claims.text: Glucocorticoids in brief courses (3 to 5 days), oral (methylprednisolone or prednisone) or IV (methylprednisolone), treat acute onset of symptoms or exacerbations that cause objective deficits sufficient to impair function
claims.quote: Glucocorticoids, given orally or intravenously in brief courses (3 to 5 days), are used to treat acute onset of symptoms or exacerbations that cause objective deficits sufficient to impair function (eg, loss of vision, strength, or coordination). Glucocorticoids may be given orally (methylprednisolone or prednisone) or intravenously (methylprednisolone).

claims.text: If glucocorticoids are ineffective in reducing an exacerbation's severity, plasma exchange may be used; it can be used for any relapsing form of MS but is not used for primary progressive MS
claims.quote: If glucocorticoids are ineffective in reducing the severity of an exacerbation, plasma exchange may be used (4). Plasma exchange can be used for any relapsing form of MS (relapsing-remitting, progressive relapsing, secondary progressive), but is not used for primary progressive MS.

claims.text: Disease-modifying therapies for relapsing-remitting MS are moderately efficacious (eg, interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, the fumarates, fingolimod) or highly efficacious (natalizumab, rituximab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, ublituximab, cladribine, alemtuzumab)
claims.quote: Disease-modifying therapies that treat relapsing remitting MS have been categorized as either moderately efficacious or highly efficacious based on their ability to reduce relapse rate, new MRI lesions, and disability: Moderately efficacious: interferon beta 1a, interferon beta 1b, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, dimethyl fumurate, monomethyl fumurate, diroximel fumarate, fingolimod, siponimod, ozanimod, ponesimod Highly efficacious: natalizumab, rituximab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, ublituximab, cladribine, and alemtuzumab.

claims.text: Ocrelizumab (anti-CD20 B-cell humanized monoclonal antibody, infused every 6 months) is effective for relapsing MS and can also be used for primary progressive MS, typically in ambulatory patients
claims.quote: Ocrelizumab, an anti-CD20 (B-cell) humanized monoclonal antibody given as an infusion every 6 months, is also effective in the treatment of relapsing MS (13). Ocrelizumab can also be used to treat primary progressive MS, typically in ambulatory patients.
